title: Chapter 213 – The Sitting Trees
html:
[Terrace Five – Veyra]

Veyra Thann has not sat under a tree in six hundred and eleven years, and she finds that she does not know what to do with her hands.

She stands at the edge of the Ripening Row with her bandaged palm pressed to her breastbone and watches the man she has agreed to protect decide whether to give up eighty years of the world. She is aware of her own breathing. It is a strange sensation, breath, after so long in stone: a small, wet, insistent rhythm, going in and out without her permission. She is aware of her heart. It runs a little fast and a little uneven, like a horse that has been rested too long. She is aware, most of all, of the second key, which lies along the whole length of her spine like a hot iron rod and hums, faintly, when she thinks of the road ahead.

She has not told the others about the hum.

She has not told them a great many things. It is one of the privileges of having been asleep, she has found. A person who has been asleep for six hundred years may be forgiven for keeping a few of her thoughts to herself.

"The Ring is gone," says Lin Jian.

---

He has been standing in front of the sitting-tree for some time, with his shaking hand tucked into his sleeve and the dead black bell in his good fist. He says it quietly, to no one in particular, in the voice of a man reading aloud from a letter he does not wish to believe. Hua turns her head. Veyra does not. She has been expecting it since the moment they walked through the gate and the golden light closed behind them like a lid.

"I felt it go," he says. "Just now. Like a rope being cut at the far end." He frowns. "There was a sound. Very small. And then everything the Ring was holding up, all at once, put itself down."

The Print, says Veyra.

"The Print is locked. The Scan is not. It was never part of the Ring." He does not look at her. "The machine says the emission has stopped."

"The leak?" Hua's voice is sharp.

"Yes. The thing at the top of the Seam can no longer hear us. Or can hear us only as it hears anyone else." He lets out a breath that is nearly a laugh. "It seems that cutting the Ring cuts the thread. I did not think of that."

Nor did the Founders, says Veyra. It was never meant to be cut from the far end.

"No." Jian lifts his head. His eyes in the golden light are very tired. "It was cut from the near end. By the people I left behind. Because they love me, and because I had stopped being able to carry them."

Nobody speaks.

The trees tick. The grass whispers. Somewhere in the long rows an amber fruit ripens and falls, and the tiny bright figure in it goes out like a spark.

Sorrel, seated on a low stool a few paces off with her basket in her lap, makes a small approving noise.

"Quiet at last," says the Keeper of the Orchard. "It was getting so very loud."

---

Veyra turns her face away, so that the hood hides her expression.

She has known men like him. She has known one man exactly like him: tall, patient, worn thin by the weight of something he refuses to put down. A man who made a bargain in a hurry and never forgave himself for the hurry. A man who stood in front of a door in the dark and said, Veyra, I will hold it. Go to sleep. I'll wake you when it's done.

He never woke her.

She thinks of this often, in the long hours of walking. She thinks of the sound of his voice, and the way he always put his hand to his sleeve when he lied.

"Lady Veyra," says Jian.

Yes.

"I am going to sit."

She does not answer at once. She has the cool, level habit of weighing a thing before she speaks, and she lets the silence stand while she examines it.

You know what you are asking, she says at last. Eighty years.

"Yes."

Of their lives. Not yours.

"Yes."

Your friends will be old when you rise. Your enemies will be dead. Your clan, if it survives, will not know your name. The girl in the nursery will be an old woman, if she lives. The man on the tower will be—

"Wenyuan is a cultivator of the Core realm," Jian says. "He will have broken through, or he will not. That is not mine to decide. It was never mine to decide." His good hand tightens on the bell. "I am not choosing eighty years. I am choosing whether to be useful at the end of them."

That is a coward's argument.

"Perhaps." He lifts his chin. "But it is the one I have."

She looks at him for a long moment. In the shadow of the hood, she lets her mouth do something she has not allowed it in six centuries. It is not quite a smile. It is the memory of one.

Sit, says Veyra Thann.

---

He sits.

The white stone bench is cool beneath him, and the tree leans in. Veyra watches the Keeper rise from her stool and cross the grass with the empty amber fruit held out in one wrinkled hand, as though offering a cup of tea. Sorrel's walnut face is grave. For once, there is no rustle in her.

"You'll feel nothing at first," she says. "It's a very slow poison. One bite of the hour and you've started. After that it's only patience."

"What is the price?"

"A year of your life, for each year you sit." Sorrel says it flatly. She is not smiling now. "The Orchard grows the hours but does not make them. I told you the trees were the engine of the Road. They are. They take what is spent, and spend it back. If you ask the tree for a year of cultivation, you pay it a year of lifespan. That is the whole bargain, and the Founders were quite proud of it."

"Ninety-one years and two hundred and thirteen days," Jian murmurs. "Less two years."

"If you are quick." The Keeper's green eyes soften. "I would be, if I were you. You have a Core at eighty-two percent and a hand that shakes. The tree will mend what it can. It cannot mend what it did not break."

He nods, once.

Veyra moves forward without deciding to. She puts her bare hand, the one with the ring of ember, on the bough above his head. The bark is warm, and faintly damp, like skin.

Lin Jian, she says.

He looks up.

I will tell you one thing, and then I will say nothing more, because I have said too much already. The cool voice is very low. The Orchard is not kind. It is fair. Those are different things. You have been treated unkindly by a great many people, and you have learned to expect fairness as a kind of mercy. Do not. It is only arithmetic.

His eyes are very dark.

"I know," he says.

Then eat.

He takes the fruit from Sorrel's hand, and bites.

---

It is not dramatic.

That is what Veyra remembers best, afterward. She expects a flare, a clap of power, the stagger of a man struck by an hour. Instead there is only the faintest golden shimmer, the sound of someone settling into a chair, and Jian's face going slack with the particular emptiness of a person who has just closed his eyes in a very deep place.

The tree above him ticks. Once. Twice. And then it falls silent, and so do the trees on either side, one after another, in a ripple that moves down the Row and out into the golden dark.

"There," says Sorrel softly. "He's gone in."

Veyra stands over him with her hand on the bough.

His breathing has slowed. It is a deep, even rhythm, a hair over four breaths to the minute, and she knows without being told that every hour he sits is forty hours in the world below. Her mind, which has always been quick with figures, turns the sum over and shows her the answer in a flat gray line.

Eighty years, she thinks. Two years in the tree.

Hua is standing at her shoulder.

She has been very quiet. Veyra has noticed this about her, the Warden's voice: when she is afraid, she goes still, the way a hare goes still in the grass. She has not spoken since Jian said the word sit. Now she looks up at the golden branches and the tiny ticking fruit, and her small face is white.

"I can't," she says.

You can.

"I can't leave the Wall for eighty years. I'm the Warden. I carry the third piece. If I—"

You will not be leaving the Wall, says Veyra. The Wall will be leaving you.

Hua flinches.

It is a cruel thing to say. I am sorry. Veyra turns, at last, and lets the hood fall back from her face. She has not done this in front of anyone since the Fourth Terrace. Under it, her skin is gray and fine, like a leaf that has lain in a book, and her eyes are the color of old river water. "I have no gift for kindness. It was never my trade. But I will tell you what I saw, in the stone, in the long dream. I saw a great many people who stood at a door and said, I cannot leave. And I saw what became of them."

What?

They did not leave. And the world went on without them. The ruined hand lifts. You will sit, Hua. You will take the next tree, and you will eat the fruit, and you will climb to the Nascent Soul in the span of a long winter. And when you rise, you will find that everything you were afraid of has already happened.

That is not comfort.

No. Veyra almost smiles. It is only the truth. Truth is the one thing I have to give.

---

Hua sits. Veyra has not the heart to watch.

But she hears it. She cannot help hearing it, in the sudden quiet of the Row: the small dry sound of the girl swallowing her fear, and the creak of the bench as she settles her back against the trunk, and the thin, steady voice, speaking the Warden's oath under her breath the way a child recites a lesson to keep the dark away.

I will hold the line. I will keep the count. I will not close my eyes while there is a name unread.

Sorrel gives her the fruit. Hua turns it over in her fingers, and the tiny bright figure inside, a girl in a plain cloak, standing at the foot of a tower, lifts her hand to the light.

"It's me," Hua says, in a voice that cracks.

"It's an hour," says the Keeper. "Yours. Take it, and you will have it back a hundredfold."

Hua bites.

Her face does not change. She lets out one long breath, and her head tips forward, and the mark in her palm dims from ember to ash and then to a pale, steady, patient gold. Veyra turns away before she can see it, because she has seen that gold before, on the faces of the Keepers of the Fourth, in the hour before the stone.

She turns instead toward the open gate, where the golden light has settled into a flat bright wall. She stands with her hands folded in her sleeves and listens to the Orchard tick. Behind her, two cultivators breathe the slow breath of the deep sitting. In front of her, the light shimmers faintly, as though someone on the far side were breathing on it.

"You are troubled," says Sorrel.

I am old.

"That is not what I said."

The Keeper has come up beside her, quiet as a leaf. She sets her basket down. There is something odd in her face, a kind of tender wariness, as of a woman who has found something unexpected in a familiar room.

"You left the bell," she says.

Yes.

"The white one. With the child in it."

I gave it to Mo Yan. She asked.

"She did not ask." Sorrel's voice is very gentle. "She was handed it. There is a difference. I have grown fruit for four hundred years and I can tell you, with the authority of long experience, that the difference is the whole of the matter."

She is a child who has paid.

"She is a child who has paid," Sorrel agrees. "She lost her mother's name for a bell that does not belong to her. She has no family but a boy of the Wall and a heavy old man with a pencil. She is nine years old and she is alone and she is carrying the one thing in the Seam that has the Bloom's attention." The green eyes are kind and very sharp. "And you left her with it."

Veyra says nothing.

She was not alone, she says at last. The Cartographer—

"The Cartographer is a tired man who draws maps."

Lan Xiu—

"Is a girl of fifteen, who was stone four days ago." Sorrel sighs. "I am not scolding you, Veyra. You have had a hard morning. I am only asking a question." She looks up, very bright and old and wrinkled, into the shadow of Veyra's face. "Why did you give it to her?"

Veyra is silent.

She thinks of Mo Yan, standing in the dust with her black bell held out like a cup, and her small stubborn face, and the way she said, without a sound: Then let us find out what it costs. She thinks of the hum in her spine. She thinks of the moment, in the arch, when she had lowered the white bell into the child's hands and felt Sera's voice leave her fingers like a bird.

Because she was not afraid, says Veyra.

"Everyone is afraid."

Not of that. She hears her own voice crack. Not of the thing in the bell. Not of the voice. She listened to it as if it were a person. A pause. I have not been able to listen to it for six hundred years. I tried. I could not. Every time I heard her, I heard what I did.

"Ah," says Sorrel.

She heard Sera. And she answered.

"What did she say?"

She said, "I'm here." Veyra closes her eyes. That is all. Nothing clever. Nothing brave. She said, "I'm here," and Sera stopped humming.

The Keeper of the Orchard does not speak for a long time.

When she does, her voice has lost the rustle and the wit. It is simply an old woman's voice, flat and tired.

"Then I think you have made a very great mistake," says Sorrel, "or the very best of your life."

Which?

"That depends," says the Keeper, "on whether the Bloom was listening."

---

Sorrel will not let her leave.

She says it plainly, with her wrinkled hands folded in her lap, when Veyra stands up from the foot of the tree and turns toward the gate. The Keeper does not rise. She does not raise her voice. She simply says, "There is no gate, my dear," and Veyra stops, because it is true.

I know.

"The stair is gone. The Fourth is gone. The Road is a road that runs one way." Sorrel's green eyes are patient. "You can go up. You cannot go down. Not until the Ninth, and the Stair-Father, and the Door. That was the Founders' last gift to the Road. Nothing that goes up may be talked out of it by a loved one at the bottom."

The child is in danger.

"The child is in danger," the old woman agrees. "She has been in danger since the day she was born. So has everyone." She tilts her head. "What would you do, if you could go down? Take the bell back? Break it? Throw it in the lake?"

I would—

She stops.

She does not know what she would do. She stands with her ruined hand at her side and her heart running fast and uneven, and the truth of it is a stone in her throat. She would hold Mo Yan. She would put her cloak around the child and take her out of the Silent Terrace and carry her down the long road to the sun. She would not be the woman who left her daughter in a bell. She would, for once, be late for nothing.

And none of it would help.

"There," says Sorrel, kindly. "You see."

I can still reach the Cartographer. Through Hua's mark.

"Through Hua's mark, which is a poor thin thread and will not last the week." The Keeper picks up her basket. "Use it while you can. Warn him. Tell him to take the child and the girl and the bell and go down, if he can, to the Wall. It is the only safe place left in the Mortal Realm."

And if he cannot?

"Then it will be as it will be," says Sorrel. "I have found that the world is rather good at that."

Veyra stands in the gold, and the ticking, and the long slow breathing of the two who sleep. She puts her hand on her spine, where the key lies, and presses.

Mo Yan, she thinks, to nobody, to the whole wide silent Road. I am sorry. I am so sorry. I am coming.

The tree above her gives a single, small, golden tick.

---

She remembers the planting.

It is not a thing she has let herself remember. But the Orchard is a place of hours, and hours have a way of coming loose from the branches when you stand too long under them, and as she watches the golden light thicken she finds that she is standing in another year, in a young orchard, with a spade in her hand.

It is spring. The trees are knee-high, thin as whips, and the Founders' engineers have laid out the rows with string and stakes. Orrin Thann is kneeling in the soil with his sleeves rolled to the elbow, and his hands are black with earth, and he is laughing.

"You have to put them in at an angle," he says. "Or they won't take the light."

"They are trees, Orrin. They do not take the light. They take the rain."

"These ones take the light. Look." He holds up a sapling, a pale green switch with a single bud, and turns it in the sun. Inside the bud there is a faint amber glow, as of a coal under ash. "The Founders say that if you plant a tree with the right intention, it keeps the intention. It remembers who put it in."

"A tree cannot remember."

"This one can." He grins. He is thirty-four years old, and tall, and awkward in the way of a man who has been a scholar too long and a husband not long enough, and there is soil on his cheek. "Come here. You do the next one."

She kneels beside him. The soil is cold and damp. She sets the sapling in the hole at the angle he showed her, and presses the earth around it with both hands, and feels, through her palms, the faintest answering pulse.

"There," he says. "Now it knows you."

"I hope it is not a gossip."

"It is a tree, Veyra. It will only say what it is told."

She does not tell him that she is afraid. She does not tell him that the Founders have asked her to bear the second key, and that she has said yes without telling him, and that she has not slept for three nights for fear of the day he finds out. She kneels in the spring dirt beside her husband and watches his hands, and thinks that it is the last perfectly ordinary afternoon she will have.

She is right.

The memory dissolves. The orchard is golden and old again; the whip-thin saplings have become twisted pewter trees; the soil under her feet is hard and dry. She has her hand pressed to her mouth. She does not know how long she has been standing there.

You planted these, she says.

"Orrin planted these," says Sorrel, behind her, very softly. "You planted the fifth row. The one where the boy is sitting."

Veyra does not turn.

I did not know the trees remembered.

"They remember everything," says the Keeper. "That is the trouble with them."

---

She does not sleep. She has not slept since the Fourth Terrace, and she does not expect to.

She sits instead on the grass beside the bench, with her back against the bole of Jian's tree, and watches the light. It has moved a little. The gold has thickened, the shadows have lengthened, and somewhere in the tree above her the ticking has taken on a new, steadier note. She is not sure what it means. She does not like not knowing.

At the second hour, she hears the hum.

It comes from her spine, and she feels it before she hears it, a thin high note like a wet finger drawn around the rim of a glass. She goes rigid. The ring of ember on her palm flares white, and the bandaged hand jerks against her chest, and she thinks, no, not now, not here, and then the note breaks and resolves into a voice.

Veyra, it says.

It is not Sera's voice. It is not Orrin's. It is an old, dry, kindly voice, with a rasp in it like a pen across parchment, and she knows it as she knows the shape of her own hands.

Cartographer, she thinks.

Forgive me for the intrusion. The voice is faint and jagged, as though shouted across a gulf. The mark is a poor channel, and the Terrace is eating my breath. I have only a moment.

What has happened?

The child.

Veyra's heart stops.

Mo Yan is well, says the Cartographer, quickly. She is asleep. She is not in danger. But she is not alone. There is something in the bell, Veyra. Not Sera. Something that wears her.

I know.

You do not know all of it. The voice cracks. I have been reading the maps. Orrin's last map, the one he sent down with the first key. I did not understand it. I understand it now.

Tell me.

It is not a map of the Road, says the Cartographer. It is a map of the Seam. And at the very center of it, marked in his own hand, with a small black circle—

The note breaks.

Veyra grips her own wrist, hard, with the bandaged hand, and feels the ember burn through the cloth.

Cartographer!

—a child's name, says the old voice, very far away, written in the place where a name should not be. Written over and over in a spiral, a thousand times. A name I have drawn once, on the back of a drawing, for a girl of nine.

Whose?

Hers, says the Cartographer. Mo Yan's.

And the hum in her spine stops, and the Orchard goes quiet, and Veyra Thann sits under the sitting tree with her ruined hand against her mouth and understands, with the cold, flat certainty of a woman who has been very wrong for a very long time, that the Bloom did not stir in the bell by accident.

It stirred because it had been given a name.
